title: Bass Lake, Indiana: the monster of Cedar Lake (1838 and 1893)
sourcing_note: Requested town (Scoop, Nov. 16, 2026: 'bass lake'). Bass Lake, Starke County. No Muse post on Bass Lake in the last two weeks (TikTok and Facebook lists read in full). This is a legend and a newspaper story, told as what the papers said. 1838: the Logansport Herald (Aug. 16), quoting McCartney, put a monster at Cedar Lake (now Bass Lake): one killed on its banks, 'the bones of which are now to be found', its mate escaped into the water; the paper called it Indian tradition, so the narration says only 'a legend' and the card quotes the paper. Two sources: Smalley's IMH article (which reprints the Herald) and Boomhower. The Telegraph's 'Lake of the Devil's Bones' name (Sept. 15, 1838) is left out: Smalley thinks editor John B. Dillon wrote these pieces playfully, and another source (a Purdue hatchery history) gives a different Indian name, 'Wichetonqua'. The Maxinkuckee 'subterranean passages' line is about Lake Manitou, not Bass Lake. 1893: the Evening Herald (Shenandoah, Pa.), June 22, 1893, p. 2, and the New Orleans Picayune, May 18, 1893 (via Charles Fort's notes) both ran the story; the Philadelphia Public Ledger (May 17) headed it 'Ananias in Indiana' (calling it a lie; not used). Four men per the Evening Herald (the Picayune says five saw it). 'A lawyer who had defended President Garfield's assassin': George Scoville led Guiteau's defense with Leigh Robinson, so 'a lawyer', not 'the lawyer'. No source says whether the monster was ever caught, so the short doesn't say. The hill and springs: Starke County History Center and Only In Your State. Time of day of the 1893 fishing trip is not given: drawn as a warm late afternoon in May (the story ran in mid-May). No one is shown hurt: the men thrown out are drawn in the air; the hook's boat is empty. Blind check Nov. 16 (script, text and pictures only): it couldn't open page 2 of the 1893 paper and leaned on a 2024 blog. Read here (page 2 OCR, panewsarchive ocr.txt): headline 'CEDAR BASS LAKE'S MONSTER' (subhead garbled, apparently '...Fish Attacks Four Men in a Boat'); 'The Cedar Bass lake monster has been seen at last'; 'The other morning Attorney Beeman, Auditor Knosman and Sheriff Vanderweele, of Knox, accompanied by Hon. George Scoville, the attorney who defended the murderer of President Garfield, went out for a fish' (as the second checker read it); Beeman's spoon bait hooked it; it 'started out for deep water with the boat' and 'gave them a free ride for half an hour'; it 'rose to the surface, whirled around' and 'struck the rear end of the boat with his tail', 'smashing the stern in a thousand pieces' and throwing 'Beeman and Knosman, who were standing in the rear end of the boat, into the water'; 'Some fishermen in a boat near by rescued Beeman and Knosman'; Vanderweele and Scoville stayed in the boat until 'their boat sank near shore in about twelve feet of water' and swam to shore; 'forty feet long and three feet thick; its head is huge and pointed'; 'greenish black'; 'devoid of any visible fins'; 'A thorough hunt for the monster will now be made.' One boat, not two: a summarizer first read 'their boat sank' as a second boat, and the pictures were briefly redrawn with two; the second check caught it, and every 'boat' clause in the article refers to the one boat (plus the rescuers' and the 1891 rowboat). Fixes after both checks: 'Something towed their boat' became 'One hooked something that towed their boat for half an hour'; the fishing pictures show four men in one boat, with the rescuers' boat nearby; at the strike two men go off the stern and two stay aboard; morning light ('The other morning'); the creature is a long finless body at the surface with a huge pointed head darting off (no raised neck or humps); the hook's boat is going down (it later sank); the hill is drawn low; line 7 became 'Bass Lake sits on a ridge with no stream flowing in. Springs and wells help fill it.' (Blatchley and Ashley, The Lakes of Northern Indiana, 1900: a basin 'on top of a ridge', 'no outlet or natural inlet', 'fed almost wholly by subaqueous springs and by the waters of flowing wells'; Starke County History Center: springs and a few flowing wells; Bass Lake Conservancy District: a pumped well puts about a million gallons a day into the lake); label 'CEDAR LAKE (NOW BASS LAKE)' (Lake County has its own Cedar Lake); the card's date line reads 'SHENANDOAH, PA., JUNE 22, 1893' (page 1 masthead). 'The papers' stays plural on the strength of Charles Fort's notes (the Picayune and the Public Ledger); no second 1893 printing was read directly. Third check Nov. 16 (the changes only): one boat confirmed clause by clause; line 5, line 7 and the card supported; no fishing rods in the article ('a heavy silk Florida line' with a spoon bait; Beeman let out about a thousand feet; 'The line was made fast'), so the fishing picture shows a hand line trailing astern and the tow picture a line made fast at the bow, no rods. It called the 1838 label unverified because it didn't read Smalley; the Herald of Aug. 16, 1838 says the lake 'is now called Cedar lake'.

sources.what: Headline 'Cedar Bass Lake's Monster': Cedar Bass Lake, near Knox, Ind., said to hold a large unseen creature (a seine torn in 1881; a rowboat capsized about two years before; a steamer pulled by something caught in its anchor line). Attorney Beeman, Auditor Knosman, Sheriff Vanderweele and attorney George Scoville went fishing; Beeman hooked something that towed the boat about half an hour; reeled near, it surfaced, turned and struck the stern with its tail, smashing it and throwing Beeman and Knosman into the water; other fishermen rescued them, Vanderweele and Scoville swam to shore. About forty feet long and three feet thick, a huge pointed head, greenish-black, no visible fins; a hunt was to follow.
sources.who: The Evening Herald (Shenandoah, Pa.), June 22, 1893, p. 2 (Pennsylvania Newspaper Archive)

sources.what: 'Monster caught in Cedar Bass Lake, near Knox, Ind. 40 feet long and 3 feet in diameter. But it got away. Five persons reported having seen it. One of them was Scoville, the lawyer who defended Guiteau.' Also the Philadelphia Public Ledger, May 17, 1893, 'Ananias in Indiana' (not used).
sources.who: New Orleans Daily Picayune, May 18, 1893, p. 4, as listed in Charles Fort's notes (resologist.net, 1893; the site loops between https and http, so read through search-result text)

sources.what: The Logansport Herald, Aug. 16, 1838, quoting Edward McCartney, said the only 'Lake Man-i-too' he knew was Cedar Lake in Stark County: 'A monster (the bones of which are now to be found) was once—so says the Indian tradition—killed on its banks, the mate of which escaped into the water.' Note 25: 'Bass Lake was called Cedar Lake by early surveyors and was known by this name for many years.' (The Telegraph's 'Lake of the Devil's Bones' name and the Maxinkuckee passages are not used: one is a joke-prone editorial claim, the other is about Lake Manitou.)
sources.who: Donald Smalley, 'The Logansport Telegraph and the Monster of the Indiana Lakes,' Indiana Magazine of History 42:3 (1946), pp. 249-267

sources.what: Logansport's Herald rejected the Telegraph's Lake Manitou monster in 1838 and promoted a different monster in Bass Lake.
sources.who: Ray E. Boomhower (senior editor, Traces of Indiana and Midwestern History), 'The Father of Indiana History and the Lake Monster' (Dec. 16, 2020)

sources.what: Bass Lake is a natural lake on top of a hill; its drainage basin slopes away from the water; underground springs and a few flowing wells keep it up (with an outlet dam level set by the Starke Circuit Court).
sources.who: Starke County History Center, 'Mysterious Bass Lake'

sources.what: Bass Lake is known for its 'lack of an obvious water source'.
sources.who: Only In Your State, 'The Most Mysterious Lake In Indiana Is Also The Most Peaceful'

sources.what: George Scoville, a Chicago lawyer and Guiteau's brother-in-law, led Charles Guiteau's defense (with Leigh Robinson) in 1881-82.
sources.who: National Park Service (James A. Garfield NHS); History.com (Christopher Klein); Encyclopedia.com, 'Charles Guiteau Trial: 1881'

sources.what: The steamer City of Kokomo ran on Bass Lake from 1892 (the 1893 story's steamer detail; not used); a Judge Beeman spoke at a launch in 1898.
sources.who: Starke County History Center, 'Bass Lake Steamers'

sources.what: Bass Lake: 'a shallow basin on top of a ridge'; drainage 'all away from its area'; 'no outlet or natural inlet'; 'fed almost wholly by subaqueous springs and by the waters of flowing wells'; formerly known as Cedar Lake.
sources.who: W. S. Blatchley and G. H. Ashley, The Lakes of Northern Indiana (Indiana Department of Geology and Natural Resources, 1900), pp. 293, 297-298 (as the second checker read it)

sources.what: A spring-fed natural lake; the district's well 'pumps about 1 million plus gallons of water into the lake per day to help keep the lake level up'.
sources.who: Bass Lake Conservancy District (as the second checker read it)

beats.text: Something in this lake smashed a fishing boat and threw two men overboard. That's what the papers said. This is Bass Lake.
beats.label: STARKE COUNTY, INDIANA
beats.credit: The Evening Herald (Shenandoah, Pa.) and New Orleans Picayune, 1893

beats.text: In 1838, when it was called Cedar Lake, a Logansport paper printed a legend.
beats.label: CEDAR LAKE (NOW BASS LAKE)
beats.credit: Indiana Magazine of History (1946), quoting the Logansport Herald, 1838

beats.text: A monster was killed on its banks, it said; its bones could still be found. Its mate escaped into the water.

lines: A monster ... was once ... killed on its banks, the mate of which escaped into the water.

beats.credit: The Logansport Herald, Aug. 16, 1838, in the Indiana Magazine of History (1946)

beats.text: In 1893, papers said four men went fishing here, among them the sheriff and a lawyer who defended President Garfield's assassin.
beats.label: THE FISHING PARTY
beats.credit: The Evening Herald (Shenandoah, Pa.) and New Orleans Picayune, 1893

beats.text: One hooked something that towed their boat for half an hour.
Then it surfaced and smashed the stern with its tail. Forty feet long, they said, greenish-black, with a huge pointed head.
beats.credit: The Evening Herald, June 22, 1893; New Orleans Picayune, May 18, 1893

beats.text: Bass Lake sits on a ridge with no stream flowing in. Springs and wells help fill it.
beats.label: BASS LAKE TODAY
beats.credit: Starke County History Center; Bass Lake Conservancy District
